transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-06-30
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez, Priya Patel (Redwood); Liam O'Neal, Sara Kim, Rajiv Menon (Skyline)

Summary:
Quick discovery on Skyline's reliability and incident tolerance needs for an LLM-based claims triage product. Focus on multi-region fallbacks, fallback policies to smaller/quantized models, SLA expectations for hosted vs dedicated, and security/audit requirements for Private deployment. Agreed to run a technical benchmark and share security docs + pricing.

Topics:
- Multi-region routing and health checks
- Fallback policies (model variants / region failover / degrade-to-text-only)
- SLA / SLO expectations and formal SLAs for Dedicated
- Private deployment considerations (VPC, KMS, audit logs)
- Cost tradeoffs: latency vs unit cost, model size switching

Action items recap at end (see metadata)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and Diego/ Priya are our SEs. How's it going?
[00:08] Liam O'Neal: Hey Maya, good thanks. We're excited, we've been evaluating a couple of options for hosting our claims triage model. Main concerns are uptime, cross-region failover, and predictable latency for SLA customers.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Great. Real quick could you share the high level constraints? P95/P99 goals, and whether you need private deployment or if hosted is ok?
[00:31] Sara Kim: Sure. Right now our target is p95 < 350ms for simple classifier calls and p99 < 800ms. For enterprise customers we promise 99.9% availability, but internally operations want us to aim for 99.95. We also have regulatory constraints for EU customers—data residency—so multi-region needed.
[00:48] Diego Alvarez: Thanks. To set expectations, Redwood Hosted typically has a 99.9% SLA for the base offering, Dedicated has an option for 99.95+ SLA depending on commit level. For the EU residency part we can region-pin requests or run Private deployment in your VPC.
[01:06] Rajiv Menon: On Private—how do you handle KMS/HSM integrations? We need key control for model inputs at rest and in-flight. Also audit logs retention for 2 years.
[01:18] Priya Patel: We integrate with customer KMS providers (AWS KMS / GCP KMS / Azure Key Vault) and support bring-your-own-key. Audit logs are available via the Console and can stream to your SIEM; retention is configurable — we'll send the SOC2 and logs retention doc.
[01:33] Liam O'Neal: For failover, are we talking DNS-level routing, or do you have a platform-level routing with health checks and automatic traffic shifting?
[01:42] Diego Alvarez: Platform-level. We run health probes per region and per model variant; routing policies can be configured by latency, cost, or priority. If a region is degraded, traffic automatically shifts to another region or a fallback model variant if the primary model isn't available. For example, you can fallback from a full 8B quantized model to a smaller 2B model or to a cached completion.
[02:05] Sara Kim: How long does routing switch take? We need near-immediate failover for critical paths.
[02:11] Diego Alvarez: It depends on the failure mode but typical near-instant is within seconds for route failover if health checks detect an outage. Bootstrapping cold models across regions can take longer; that's why we recommend warm-standby or pre-warmed model variants in the secondary region for low-latency failover.
[02:27] Liam O'Neal: Could you explain warm standby a bit more? We're concerned about cost of pre-warming.
[02:33] Priya Patel: Warm-standby means reserved capacity in the secondary region with a smaller fleet or lower concurrency, ready to scale up quickly. Redwood Dedicated supports reserved GPU pools that you can autoscale, and you can configure burst policies. We also offer a degraded execution mode — fall back to a lighter quantized variant to preserve latency and keep service available while reducing cost.
[02:52] Rajiv Menon: Are there options for multi-region active-active vs active-passive setups? We want active-active for EU + US to reduce cross-region latencies.
[03:00] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we support active-active. Requests can be routed to the nearest region using geolocation policies, and KV cache propagation is handled via async replication to reduce cross-region read latency. Note: KV cache is eventually consistent — sometimes transcriptions show 'KV cash' in our notes, apologies — but for most inference workloads it works fine.
[03:20] Sara Kim: That eventual consistency is okay for our use case as long as there are clear docs. Any chance of model state/kv cache conflicts?
[03:27] Priya Patel: Conflicts are rare; we recommend stateless request patterns where possible. For chat-like memory you can pin session affinity to a region or use sticky sessions.
[03:36] Liam O'Neal: What happens under an infrastructure-level incident? Let's say a cloud region has a zonal outage—what's user-visible and how do you prevent cascading failures?
[03:47] Diego Alvarez: We have guardrails: circuit breakers at the router, per-tenant rate limiting, and prioritized queuing. If a region is flapping, the router will progressively shift traffic away before a full failover, to prevent overloading the secondary. We also can apply automatic model degradation: reduce model size or throttle non-critical routes.
[04:07] Rajiv Menon: About SLO/SLA — you said Dedicated has a 99.95 option. What about financial credits and how they're calculated?
[04:14] Maya Chen: For Dedicated we have tiered SLAs tied to committed capacity. Credits are pro-rated based on downtime minutes and pledged throughput. We'll include the formal SLA language in the docs we send. Hosted API has a standard 99.9 SLA with different credits for partial outages.
[04:30] Sara Kim: Do you do canary rollouts and automatic rollback on quality regressions? We can't afford to push a model that suddenly changes behavior.
[04:38] Diego Alvarez: Yes. Rolling deploys, canaries, and automatic rollback on error rates or quality regressions are supported. We also tie quality monitoring to prompt sets and can alert on regression deltas. Many customers run a canary at 1-5% before full rollout.
[04:54] Liam O'Neal: From a compliance perspective, how granular is audit logging? We need per-request metadata (who, what model, model version, region, latency).
[05:03] Priya Patel: Per-request meta is supported. Logs include request id, model version, region, user token id, latency, and outcome codes. Logs can be forwarded to S3 / GCS or your SIEM. Retention can be configured and we support export for audits.
[05:16] Rajiv Menon: Are there any additional network controls? We run private subnets and strict egress policies.
[05:21] Diego Alvarez: For Private deployment we hand over a customer-managed control plane in your VPC, so egress rules are under your control. For Hosted/Dedicated we offer VPC peering and private endpoints; you can restrict outbound traffic.
[05:33] Sara Kim: Performance testing—how would a benchmark look if we run 100 RPS with 256 token average? What should we expect for p95?
[05:42] Diego Alvarez: Depends on model size and instance type. For a 2B model on Dedicated M40-like instances, p95 might be ~200-300ms under 100 RPS with batching. For 8B quantized it could be 400-700ms. We'll propose a benchmark matrix and run it in your environment or in our dedicated sandbox.
[06:02] Liam O'Neal: On the subject of batching, how do you control latency vs throughput? We don't want batching to cause latency spikes.
[06:09] Priya Patel: The runtime uses dynamic batching and latency SLO-aware throttles; you can set max latency targets per route and the runtime will prioritize. There's also intelligent batching windows — short windows for low-latency routes.
[06:21] Sara Kim: Any limitations on model fallback compatibility? If we pick a model in the 8B family, can fallback automatically go to a different architecture model?
[06:30] Diego Alvarez: Fallback works best within compatible families but we can map fallbacks to different but functionally similar variants. There is some nuance for tokenization/behaviour differences; we recommend regression tests for fallback flows.
[06:44] Liam O'Neal: Cost question — if we keep warm-standby in a second region, how does billing work? Is it always charged at reserved rate?
[06:52] Maya Chen: Reserved capacity is billed based on your commit; warm-standby can be part of reserved capacity or on-demand. We can model costs for both scenarios and show break-even points. We'll include examples in the pricing doc.
[07:03] Rajiv Menon: Regarding incident reporting and post-mortems, do you share timelines and root cause analyses?
[07:09] Priya Patel: Yes. For Dedicated and Private we commit to incident reports with timelines and RCAs. Hosted customers get high-level incident summaries and can request a deeper report for major incidents.
[07:20] Liam O'Neal: It'd be good to see some sample routing policy config.
[07:24] Diego Alvarez: We'll send a sample config with geo, latency, and cost-based priorities. Example: primary region eu-west-1, secondary us-east-1, fallback to quantized-2B model after 500ms or 3 failed probes.
[07:38] Sara Kim: One more—how do you test multi-region failover without impacting production?
[07:43] Diego Alvarez: We recommend a staged rehearsal: run failover in a canary namespace or simulate region failure in a staging account. We provide tooling to simulate health check failures so you can observe behavior.
[07:55] Liam O'Neal: Ok that's helpful. Timeline-wise, we want to pilot in staging in July and potentially go to Dedicated in Q4. Security signoff is the gating factor.
[08:05] Maya Chen: Great. We'll send the SOC2, SOC3 if needed, dedicated pricing and benchmark plan. Diego will follow up to schedule the benchmark session.
[08:12] Sara Kim: Sounds good. Also Rajiv will share the network diagrams and retention requirements.
[08:18] Rajiv Menon: Yep I'll upload that to the shared drive after this.
[08:23] Diego Alvarez: Quick note — in case of a severe incident we can route to a degraded read-only mode or to cached responses to keep the UI responsive while we triage. Many customers prefer UX continuity over correctness for short windows.
[08:37] Liam O'Neal: Makes sense. Any blockers from our perspective today? Not that I see.
[08:42] Maya Chen: Ok last recap of next steps — Maya will email docs and pricing, Diego will schedule benchmark, Rajiv and Sara will share infra + traffic patterns, and we'll reconvene after the benchmark.
[08:56] Liam O'Neal: Thanks everyone. Appreciate the practical answers.
[09:00] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had occasional word swaps (e.g., "KV cash" / "KV cache") and speaker labels sometimes generic; timestamps approximate.
